newsitem.title: USA: TWA crash searchers scraping ocean floor.
newsitem.headline: TWA crash searchers scraping ocean floor.

text.p: Investigators seeking to find the cause of the TWA Flight 800 disaster began dredging part of the crash site on Monday for the remaining pieces of the downed jet's wreckage, a spokeswoman said.

Private trawling ships, contracted through the U.S. Navy, started the operation in a one square mile (2.5 sq km) area in the ocean off New York's Long Island, said Shelly Hazle, a spokeswoman for the National Transporation Safety Board.

"They're doing scallop trawling in a one-mile-square box furthest away from the airport," Hazle said. "It's a rake that can penetrate 6-10 inches (15-25 cm) into the sand and silt, scooping the debris up in nets."

Investigators recovered more than 95 percent of the plane's wreckage but said they did know what caused the Paris-bound jet to explode and crash just minutes after taking off from Kennedy International Airport on July 17.
All 230 people on board died in the disaster, which investigators believed was caused either by a bomb, a missile or mechanical failure.

The spokeswoman said searchers were concerned aircraft wreckage might have been shifted by hurricanes that swept up the U.S. east coast in September. She said crash investigators would evaluate the success of the dredging in coming days before deciding whether to expand the trawling area.
Officials noted that the trawling marked a turning point in the investigation because the process will irretrievably damage the crash site.
U.S. Navy divers using high-powered sonar equipment finished their search of the crash site on Saturday, marking the occasion with a memorial service for the flight's victims.

Investigators were reassembling parts of the plane in an old airplane hangar in Calverton, New York, focusing on the Boeing 747's centre fuel tank, which exploded. However, significant parts of the tank remained missing.
